subject: English
title: A Bottle of Dew
summary: Rama Natha believes in a magic potion that can turn things into gold. A sage guides him into years of honest work on a banana plantation, teaching him that hard work and perseverance create real wealth.
content:
Overview
A Bottle of Dew is a fable about Rama Natha, a man who believes that a magical potion can turn objects into gold. The story shows that success does not come from shortcuts or magic, but from patience, hard work and perseverance.

Story Explanation
1. Rama Natha's belief
Rama Natha inherits large areas of land but spends his time searching for a magic potion. People cheat him by promising to reveal the secret. His wife Madhumati worries about the money he is wasting.

2. The sage's plan
Sage Mahipati tells Rama Natha to plant banana plants, care for them himself and collect morning dew from their leaves. He must collect five litres of dew.

3. Years of hard work
Rama Natha cleans his unused fields and plants many banana plants. He cares for them and collects dew during winter. Madhumati helps by selling the bananas in the market. After six years, Rama Natha has collected five litres of dew.

4. The truth
Rama Natha takes the bottle to Mahipati. The sage appears to perform magic, but the liquid does not turn a copper vessel into gold. Rama Natha becomes angry because he thinks he has wasted six years.

5. What Rama Natha learns
Mahipati reveals that there was no magic potion. Rama Natha and Madhumati created their wealth by working on the land, growing bananas and selling the harvest. Rama Natha understands the lesson and decides to work even harder.

Key Characters
• Rama Natha — initially searches for an easy way to become rich but learns the value of hard work.
• Madhumati — his worried but supportive wife who helps sell the harvest.
• Sage Mahipati — uses a clever plan to teach Rama Natha.

What We Learn
Perseverance, diligence and honest work are more valuable than shortcuts. The story encourages us to recognise the value of effort.

Vocabulary
• plantation — land where crops are grown
• potion — a liquid believed to have special properties
• dew — small drops of water that form on leaves
• tended — looked after carefully
• wisdom — deep understanding or good judgement

Summary
Rama Natha searches for a magical way to become rich, but Mahipati makes him work on a banana plantation. Rama Natha and Madhumati earn money by growing and selling bananas. He finally learns that their wealth came from their own effort, not magic.

subject: English
title: The Raven and the Fox
summary: Reynard the Fox uses flattering words to make a raven open its beak and drop its food. The fable teaches students to be careful about excessive praise and not let pride control their actions.
content:
Overview
The Raven and the Fox is a fable in poetic form. A raven has a piece of food in its beak when Reynard the Fox notices it. The fox uses praise and flattery to make the raven sing, causing the food to fall.

Poem Explanation
1. The Raven has the food
Mr Raven is sitting on a tree branch with a morsel of food in his beak. Reynard wants the food and looks for a clever way to get it.

2. The Fox uses flattery
The Fox praises the Raven and calls him handsome. He admires the Raven's feathers and says that if the Raven sings, the birds of the woods would call him King.

3. The Raven is fooled
The Raven becomes proud and forgets that his voice is a croak. He opens his beak to sing, and the food falls down.

4. The Fox gets the food
The Fox laughs and takes the food. The Raven learns that sweet words and excessive praise can make a person act foolishly.

Key Characters
• Mr Raven — proud and influenced by flattering praise.
• Reynard the Fox — clever and cunning, using praise to get the food.

Theme and Message
The fable warns against vanity and flattery. We should think carefully about why someone is praising us instead of allowing praise to control our decisions.

Vocabulary
• raven — a large black bird
• morsel — a small piece of food
• flattery — excessive praise used to influence someone
• croak — the rough sound made by a raven
• vanity — excessive pride in one's appearance or abilities

Language Focus
The poem uses rhyme, such as limb–him and joke–croak. The NCERT activities also ask students to identify rhyming words and retell the poem as a story or conversation.

Summary
Reynard wants the food held by Mr Raven. He praises the Raven and asks him to sing. The proud Raven opens his beak, the food falls, and the Fox gets it. The fable teaches that excessive pride and flattering words can lead to poor decisions.
